system.description:
Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

Works only outdoors. It calls one normal woodland creature from within a mile of the caster; the creature saves versus spell to resist. The DM picks the kind of creature by the terrain and the caster's level, and its hit dice can be no more than half the caster's level.

  • The beast is friendly and stays with the shukenja while he travels in the wilderness, but won't go more than 20 miles from its home. When he enters a large camp, village or other settlement, it leaves him. Mistreating it makes it leave, or even turn on him.
  • There is no telepathy or perfect communication, but it understands the general meaning of spoken commands and gestures. It is still a wild beast and can be dangerous, especially if it mistakes an ordinary situation for a threat.
  • Treated well, it defends and serves him as best its ability and nature allow: a monkey prefers tricks and harassment to open combat, while a tiger springs fearlessly among his foes. Monkeys, hawks, badgers, boars, bears, tigers and serpents are common.

Material component: a piece of candy, sugar or another tasty morsel for the creature.

OA p.57. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

The shukenja tries to learn whether some action in the next three turns will turn out well or badly. The chance of success is 70% plus 1% per level. The DM gives the answer, always in general terms; precise details are never revealed. Material component: a set of straight willow sticks or carved bones.

OA p.57. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

The shukenja is wrapped in an aura of mystic harmony and wisdom. Everyone who sees him knows him for a holy man of virtue and kindness, and many are inclined to treat him in a friendly, respectful way: +20% on encounter reaction rolls with most non-player characters and creatures.

  • Sworn enemies of the character, his race, his class or what he stands for are immune.
  • It doesn't work on creatures who have no idea of his position or role: a den of tigers or bandits waiting in ambush aren't affected, but peasants, or a village of ninja (if they haven't been hired to harm him), are.
  • Those affected keep their free will and don't simply follow his suggestions; their reactions improve for everyday dealings, not for very unusual events.

OA p.57. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

Friendly creatures not yet in combat get +1 to hit. The reverse, curse, gives unfriendly creatures -1 to hit.

OA p.57. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Soothes a mind troubled by fear, temporary insanity, confusion or other mental distress, ending the effect and restoring the recipient's normal state of mind. The shukenja points at the recipient and recites a few holy scriptures. Because his distress makes him unwilling, the recipient saves versus spell: if he saves, the spell fails; if he fails, he is calmed. Material component: a prayer wheel or a page of sutras.

OA p.57. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

By touch, the shukenja heals 1-8 points of damage on a living creature with a solid body. The reverse, cause light wounds, does 1-8 points of damage.

OA p.57. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

The shukenja, or any creature in range, is wrapped in a mystic shield against missiles and blows. Against any attack that hits, the protected creature saves versus death: on a success it takes no damage from a missile weapon, or half damage from a melee attack, having nimbly stepped aside or turned the blow.

The reverse, attraction, is cast on an unwilling foe, who saves versus spell to avoid it. If he fails, each time he is hit he takes 1 extra point of damage per level of the caster, unless he makes a second save versus death for that hit.

OA p.57. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Shows whether a creature (or object) carries a disease, normal or magical, with a 10% chance per level of identifying the exact disease. Material component: a bamboo wand with paper strips inscribed with prayers.

OA p.58. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Detects evil, or good when reversed. Nonmagical objects and unintelligent creatures don't radiate evil. Material component: the shukenja's holy symbol.

OA p.58. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Gives general information on the balance of forces (good, evil, law and chaos) in an area: not the exact alignment or nature of anything, only the general proportions. The DM answers from what he knows of the target, always vaguely ("there is more evil than good here", "the lawful order of the universe is strong here").

  • On a living creature, it counts not just its alignment but its deeds, its present intentions and anything else at odds with its stated alignment: a lawful evil character known for occasional bursts of compassion for the helpless might read as "faithful, but with the other forces at struggle".
  • On buildings and areas, it shows whether powers are at work there: a house haunted by spirits leans toward evil and destruction; the cave of a famous holy hermit gives the opposite impression.

Material component: a specially prepared scroll of sutras costing 25 gp for paper and inks.

OA p.58. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

The shukenja detects magical radiation, even through solid things; stone 1 foot thick, metal 1/12 foot thick or wood 3 feet thick blocks it. Material component: his holy symbol.

OA p.58. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Shows whether an object has been poisoned or is poisonous. One item can be checked per round; large areas may take several rounds. Material component: a sprig of holly.

OA p.58. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Finds common things or forces of nature hidden from view: water, buried treasure, stolen goods and the like. The shukenja names what he seeks and holds a wand cut from a ginkgo tree (the material component) in both hands. If the thing is in range, the wand points toward it and pulls him along; if it meets an obstacle it can't pass (the ground, say), it presses against it and stops. If nothing matching is in range, the wand doesn't react, though he can move about searching.

OA p.58. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Reveals the common name, background, lineage and deeds of a creature, object or place, if it has any notable history. It doesn't reveal secret identities, magic, magical abilities, alignment and so on.

  • On a character: his parents, his family, and his ancestors' famous deeds.
  • On an object: its name (if it has one), notable deeds it took part in, and its maker. A katana might be revealed as "the Cloud-Cutting Sword, used by the great hero Akicha Tanokura at the Battle of the Fallen Bridges, made for him by the master swordsmith Lei Yung".
  • A disguised or polymorphed creature saves versus spell; if it fails, the spell works normally. It has no effect on disguised or polymorphed objects or places.
  • The caster must see the creature, handle the object, or stand within the grounds of the place.

Material component: a pair of carved bones.

OA p.58. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Foretells the general fortune of a major undertaking. The shukenja asks a deity for a sign about the plan; the casting itself is quick, but he must stay in one place watching the natural world around him for the whole casting time. Then he sees an omen (a flight of birds, an animal, a falling leaf) showing the undertaking's general fortune. It is often cast before a journey, a major battle or some notable feat.

  • The DM first weighs the plan against what only he knows. For example, the characters plan to leave a village to punish bandits in the mountains, but the DM knows the bandits will attack the village that night: an ill omen, since the characters wouldn't find the bandits.
  • With nothing to go on, he rolls 1d10 on Table 63 below (also the roll table "OA Table 63: Divination Results").
  • Omens are rare and hard to read, and the strain allows the spell only once a week.
d10Result
1-2Ill omen: the characters shouldn't undertake the task today. If they ignore the advice, all are -1 on to-hit and saving throw rolls for the rest of the day, their chance of encounters is doubled, and all encounters have a -10% reaction modifier.
3-4Great danger: the chance of encounters is doubled for the day, all encounters have a -10% reaction modifier, and foes are +1 to hit.
5-7Neutral omen: no special modifiers.
8-9Favorable omen: the characters can travel half again their normal rate today, and foes are -1 to hit them today.
10Auspicious omen: all the effects of a favorable omen, and +1 on all saving throws today.

OA Table 63: Divination Results.

OA p.58. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Makes rotten, spoiled, poisoned or contaminated food and water safe to eat and drink. The reverse, putrefy food and drink, does exactly the opposite.

OA p.59. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

Hardens the recipient against the pains and discomforts of heat, cold, fatigue and hunger.

  • Normal heat and cold don't affect him, and he takes 1 point less per die from magical fire and cold (ice, cold rays and so on).
  • Fatigue is banished as if he had slept an hour per level of the caster (this doesn't let spellcasters regain spells).
  • The effects of hunger and starvation are put off until the spell ends.

Material components: a piece of rice cake or dumpling, a scrap of cloth, a drop of water and an owl's feather.

OA p.59. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

A hypnotic pattern makes one or more snakes stop everything except swaying half-upright. It lasts 3-6 turns if the snakes are in a torpor, 1-3 turns if they are active but not attacking, and 5-8 melee rounds if they are angry or attacking. The total hit points of snakes affected can't exceed the shukenja's hit points, whether one snake or many.

OA p.59. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

The shukenja enters a deep trance in which he can't move, speak or act, but is closely tuned to the powers and forces around him, learning whether supernatural or magical effects are at work in the area. Each round of trance, he senses the presence of one lesser spirit, greater spirit, curse, permanent magical effect or haunting in the area, and its general type (a nature spirit, an evil haunting and so on), but can't communicate with it or learn anything else about it.

For example, a party stops for the night at a deserted temple. The shukenja enters a trance and learns that an evil spirit haunts it; the party can prepare defenses or leave.

OA p.59. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

Prepares one weapon to fight a particular foe. The shukenja carefully writes on the weapon who the foe is, with several sutras to give it power. He needn't know the foe's name, but must identify one specific character or creature: "a kappa" isn't enough, but "the kappa who lives in Ch'i Sheng's millpond" is.

  • The weapon is then +5 to hit and damage on its first attack against that foe, and counts as magical for hitting creatures harmed only by magical weapons.
  • It doesn't add to a magical weapon's bonus: on a +2 weapon the effect is still +5, not +7.
  • If the weapon strikes another creature while the spell lasts, the blade is wiped clean and the spell is lost.

Material component: a writing brush and ink made from dragon's blood.

OA p.59. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

The recipient gets the benefit of bless plus 1-8 extra hit points, which can take him above his normal total and are the first lost in combat (once lost, they can't be restored by curing). Material components: a strip of white cloth with the recipient's name written on it and sticky at both ends, and the shukenja's holy symbol.

OA p.59. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

When the chant is complete, all the shukenja's allies in the area are +1 on attacks, damage and saving throws, and all his foes -1. The effects last only while he keeps chanting; any movement or attack on him interrupts the spell.

OA p.59. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

The shukenja contacts one of the hundreds of local spirits in the land: spirits of limited range and power, the lesser spirits (see the OA Lite Monsters), such as the spirit of a particular tree, rock or stream, typical lesser nature spirits, or a spirit haunting one building or compound. The spirit of a mountain or river is greater and beyond this spell. He must know the spirit's identity (a trance spell can find it) and be within 10 feet of where it lives.

  • He can ask one question per level of experience. Questions must be specific and clearly worded, but needn't be yes-or-no.
  • The spirit answers literally and volunteers nothing. Its answers are always correct if it knows them. Good spirits try to be as helpful as the limits allow; neutral spirits answer in riddles or roundabout ways; evil spirits always try to twist the answer by the question's wording.
  • It can answer only about the immediate area it affects; questions beyond its scope are wasted. The spirit of a great tree in a village knows nothing of events outside the village; a ghost haunting a temple can't discuss anything unrelated to the temple or its reasons for haunting. The DM decides what falls within the spirit's realm.
  • The DM can limit the spell to once a week (or less) for any one spirit, since spirits don't like being bothered by the trifling affairs of the material world.

Material components: incense, and an offering suited to the spirit's nature.

OA p.59. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

A spring of fresh, clear, cool water bubbles up at the shukenja's command, only from natural rock or earth (never from creatures, plants or made things), giving 1 gallon per level per turn. The reverse, dry spring, reduces the flow of any natural or created spring by the same amount. Material component: a bamboo cane.

OA p.60. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Shows whether a creature is under a charm spell. Someone charmed by a creature gets a saving throw; if he succeeds, no charm is detected. The reverse shields one creature completely from this detection.

OA p.60. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Shows whether a creature is alive, including creatures in feign death, a coma or a trance. Any mental protection blocks it, as does any thickness of metal; an inch of stone or wood counts as 10 feet of open space. Material component: the shukenja's holy symbol.

OA p.60. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

The shukenja falls into a deep sleep and dreams of places and events around him: what is happening there as he dreams, not the past or future. His spirit goes where he wishes, seeing and hearing and moving normally.

  • His dream spirit passes through solid objects freely but can't enter an area guarded by any protection spell (good, neutral or evil), nor hear sounds from one.
  • It moves up to 36" a round, then can watch the scene around it the next round. A 3rd level shukenja could send it up to 72" in the first two rounds and spend the third (and last) watching.
  • At the end of the spell it returns automatically to his body; he can also return early by choice.
  • If his body is disturbed before the spirit returns, he saves versus death. On a success the spirit returns safely; on a failure the body falls into a deep catatonic state and the spirit can't return by itself. Another shukenja can use dream sight to guide the lost spirit back, if he can find it.
  • While dreaming, his spirit counts as a lesser spirit for all purposes: it can be forced to answer questions by commune with lesser spirit, can't see what invisibility to spirits hides, and can be destroyed by smite. If it is destroyed, his body falls into a catatonic state lifted only by raise dead, resurrection, limited wish or wish.

Material component: a stick of incense worth at least 5 gp.

OA p.60. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

The shukenja holds a group's attention and wins a positive response. He must speak without interruption for one round, and the listeners must fully understand the language. They save to resist; those of a race unfriendly to the caster save at +4. Beings of more than 4 hit dice, or with wisdom 15 or more, are unaffected.

  • It lasts up to six turns, as long as he keeps speaking.
  • Those who fail listen as if he had charisma 21; those who save treat him as having charisma 3.
  • Any discussion of politics, religion or alignment gives a new saving throw at +5.

OA p.60. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Holds 1-3 human or humanoid creatures motionless. Each target saves, at -1 if two are targeted and -2 if only one. Only humanoid creatures are affected. Material component: a small sphere of iron.

OA p.60. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Turns a previously crafted item into a holy symbol. It must be made of materials suited to the shukenja's deity, and he can make holy symbols only of his own deity. A shukenja can carry up to two holy symbols at a time. A holy symbol radiates good or evil, by his alignment.

OA p.60. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

The caster senses the basic needs, drives and emotions of any unshielded mind: hunger, fear, greed, love, anger, hatred and so on. Minds protected from detection by spells, magic items or psionic powers give nothing, and it doesn't work on mindless creatures (slimes, oozes, jellies, unthinking undead and most plants). The reverse, conceal motivation, masks the emotions and drives of the creature it is cast on. Material component: a prayer written on a strip of cloth tied around the caster's forehead.

OA p.61. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

The shukenja uses a small animal or semi-intelligent creature at hand as a messenger. He gives it simple directions and ties an item or note to it; it follows the directions and, if told to, waits there until the spell ends. Material component: a bit of food to lure the animal.

OA p.61. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Mist rises around the shukenja, cutting all vision to 2 to 8 feet. A strong wind cuts the duration by 75%.

OA p.61. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

An invisible barrier surrounds the recipient, keeping most spirits out of the circle.

  • Lesser spirits can't enter, though they can still shoot missiles and cast spells into it. They are -2 to hit, and those inside get +2 on saving throws against their magical attacks.
  • Greater spirits can enter with a successful save versus death, one try per spirit; on a failure that spirit can't break the barrier. They are -1 on all to-hit rolls, and those inside get +1 on saving throws against their magical attacks. A greater spirit that gets inside is also -1 on all saving throws.

The OA Lite Monsters say which spirits are lesser and which greater. Material component: a ginkgo wand with paper prayer strips attached.

OA p.61. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

The shukenja asks a spirit for a service or deed. He must know the spirit's identity first and be in the area it occupies. The request must be within the spirit's powers: the lesser nature spirit of a stream could be asked to change its course a little or bring fish to a certain place; the Lord of the Sea could be asked to raise a great storm, bring back something from the depths, or give a ship smooth sailing.

  • The spirit always saves versus spell; if it saves, it needn't heed the request. A request beyond its powers fails. The DM can rule that in special cases the request is followed automatically, especially where refusing would cause great harm to the spirit.
  • Word it carefully: the spirit follows the literal wording, not the intent. Asking for a great storm without saying where and when won't get the result wanted. The spirit will also try to harm the caster (or put him under some obligation), usually by twisting the request, since he is bothering it.
  • The spell is exhausting. Afterward the shukenja is mentally and physically drained: all memorized spells are forgotten and can't be regained until he has had a full week of rest. In that time he can travel, but can't take part in combat except to use magic items that need no concentration or physical effort. His hit points drop to 1, and lost hit points can be regained only by cure spells (cast by someone else) or magic items.

Material component: an offering of suitable value to the spirit, from 25 to 500 gp, which must also mean something to the spirit (usually a work of art or of fine craftsmanship; plain cash is seldom enough). The DM decides the nature and value of the offering.

OA p.61. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

Slows the effects of poison in the person touched, keeping him alive for the duration. The poison isn't neutralized: he loses 1 hit point a turn, down to 1 hit point, while the spell lasts. If he hasn't been cured by the end, he dies. Material components: the shukenja's holy symbol and a bud of garlic.

OA p.61. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Calls all snakes, serpents and serpent-like creatures in the area. Creatures with more hit dice than the shukenja's level, or with high intelligence, save versus spell to avoid it. Those who fail (or get no save) come to the shukenja and follow him while he keeps concentrating, and don't try to harm him or those with him unless attacked; an attack breaks the spell. He can move at half speed without breaking concentration. At the end, the serpents return to their normal state, with whatever results that brings. Material component: a small silver flute, played for the whole duration.

OA p.61. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

system.aoe: One animal within 3" radius of caster
system.description:
The shukenja can talk with any normal, non-fantastic warm- or cold-blooded creature of intelligence 1 or more. The animals don't attack while the spell lasts.

OA p.61. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

Sharpens the recipient's awareness of danger.

  • His chance of being surprised by events within the area drops by one (1-2 in 6 becomes 1 in 6, and so on). A missile shot from outside the area can still surprise him.
  • Within the same limits he can't be struck from behind, since he is automatically aware of anything moving behind him.
  • 30% chance he automatically notices any trap or hidden danger (including invisible foes) in the area.
  • Any foe in the area has half the normal chance to hide in shadows or move silently.

Only the recipient notices the warnings; it is up to him whether to tell the rest of his group. Material component: a small metal figure sprinkled with the dust of a crushed pearl.

OA p.62. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

The shukenja changes the flow of time for himself alone: 1 segment of outside time equals 1 round for him. It lasts 2 outside segments plus 1 per level (2 rounds plus 1 per level, from his point of view). While withdrawn he may read, think, meditate, and cast informational spells such as augury, or curing spells on himself only. Any other action, including walking, becoming invisible or curing others, ruins the spell. Material component: a small scroll of rice paper.

OA p.62. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

A blasting rebuke on the shukenja's foes, its effect depending on each victim's alignment compared with his:

  • Same alignment: save versus spell or be deafened for 1-3 rounds by his blistering words.
  • One part different (law, neutrality, chaos, good or evil): 1 point of damage per level of the caster, or 1/2 point per level on a successful save versus spell.
  • Both parts different: 1-4 points per level of the caster, half on a successful save.

So a lawful good shukenja deafens lawful good victims, does 1 point per level to lawful neutral, lawful evil, chaotic good and neutral good, and 1-4 per level to true neutral, neutral evil, chaotic neutral and chaotic evil. Material component: the shukenja's holy symbol.

OA p.62. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Permanently cures most forms of blindness. The reverse, cause blindness, blinds the target unless he makes a saving throw.

OA p.62. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Cures most diseases: the sufferer returns to full health in one turn to one week, depending on the disease. The reverse, cause disease, takes effect in 1-6 turns: the victim loses 1 hit point a turn and 1 strength point an hour until down to 10% of his original hit points and strength. The shukenja must touch the victim, who must fail his saving throw.

OA p.62. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Brings an unconscious human or demi-human at -1 to -9 hit points up to 0 hit points, stopping the bleeding and deterioration; further curing then restores consciousness. Material components: the shukenja's holy symbol, a scrap of white silk and any kind of ointment.

OA p.62. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

The shukenja has a 5% chance per level of detecting any cursed item, person or place. He can check one man-sized object or one square yard of area each round. Once a cursed item is found, he has the same chance of learning the general nature of the curse, though not its exact triggers and effects: scanning a cursed scroll, he might learn that it brings the reader misfortune, but not that it lowers the reader's saving throws and to-hit rolls by 1 until removed. He can check each item or area only once, however many times he casts the spell. Material components: a gem worth at least 10 gp (given to his deity as an offering) and a fresh spray of cherry or plum blossoms.

OA p.62. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

Neutralizes any magic it touches. The base chance is 50%, +5% for each level the shukenja is above the level of the magic, -2% for each level below. It automatically ends his own magic. It affects potions (as 12th level magic), but not other magic items unless cast specifically on that item; then the item gets a saving throw only if a creature is holding it, and on a failure stops working for one round. Artifacts and relics aren't affected.

OA p.62. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Gathers information about an area whose location is known: the relative strength of creatures there, the amount and value of treasure, and whether the area is watched by supernatural beings. The chance of a correct divination is 60% plus 1% per level, adjusted by the DM as needed; an incorrect divination gives wrong information. Material components: a handful of coins, incense and the shukenja's holy symbol; powerful divinations may need jewelry or magic items.

OA p.62. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Sends a message to someone in a dream. As he begins, the shukenja names the recipient; he must know who it is, or name him by a title that leaves no doubt. He could send a dream to the governor of Changtai Province without ever having met him, since there is only one, but not to "the sake-maker" of a village in that province, since there might be several.

  • After the one-turn casting, he falls into a deep, trance-like sleep, and his spirit travels instantly to the recipient and enters his dreams, unless the recipient is magically protected from spirits.
  • If the recipient is awake, the shukenja can stay in his trance until he sleeps, or cancel the spell. He learns nothing of the recipient's activities or whereabouts, only whether he is asleep or awake.
  • In the dream he delivers a message of any length, which the recipient remembers perfectly on waking. It is one-way: the recipient can't answer or ask questions, and the shukenja learns nothing from the recipient's dreams.
  • Once the message is delivered, his spirit returns instantly to his body. If his body is disturbed in any way during the spell, his spirit is lost, and his body stays in a coma until some way is found to rejoin them, such as a restore spell.
  • The spell lasts as long as it takes to enter the recipient's dreams and deliver the message: a round, or several hours.

The reverse, nightmare, sends a hideous, unsettling vision. The victim must be identified as above and asleep. He saves versus spell to avoid it; if he fails, he gets no restful sleep, loses 1d10 hit points, wakes as tired as if he hadn't slept, and can't regain spells.

Material components: a bowl of incense and a robe of red (white for the reverse) silk cloth.

OA p.63. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Sohei can use this spell (OA Table 62).

The caster can withstand normal fire and gets +2 on all saving throws against magical fire. For each level above 5th, he may affect one more man-sized creature (or equal mass). Material components: a powdered ruby and the shukenja's holy symbol.

OA p.63. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Makes the shukenja, or anyone he touches, invisible to spirits of all kinds; he can move among them unnoticed, though other creatures see him perfectly well. If he attacks, the spirits affected by the attack can see him at once. Items picked up after the spell is cast, and visible magical effects, aren't invisible to spirits. Material components: a writing brush and a jar of red ink, with which the shukenja writes sutras on every part of the person made invisible.

OA p.63. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Reads the exact alignment of one person (human or nonhuman) per round. The reverse, obscure alignment, hides the alignment of one person for a turn, two for 5 rounds, and so on.

OA p.63. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Levitates the shukenja or another creature, up to 1,000 gp (100 lb.) per level. He can move himself up or down 20 feet a round, or another creature 10 feet a round (an unwilling target saves to avoid it). No horizontal movement is possible, and the caster can end it at will. Material component: a small kite and string.

OA p.63. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Works only in a temple of the shukenja's deity or on other ground holy to his faith. His clothing protects him like chain mail, with a +1 enchantment for every four levels, if he wears no other armor or protective device. It ends if he is knocked unconscious or leaves the area.

OA p.63. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

The shukenja tries to force a deed or behavior on an unwilling creature in return for some consideration from him (usually sparing its life). The creature must understand his speech.

  • The oath must be limited to things the creature can do with its natural abilities, and can't directly cause harm to it or another. He could make a highwayman swear never to rob again, an evil monster return to the deserted lands it came from, or a lord never again overtax his peasants; he couldn't demand that a monster kill itself, or force a samurai to attack a camp of dangerous monsters. The DM decides whether an oath goes beyond these limits.
  • The victim saves versus spell to avoid it, at -2 if he was subdued in combat.
  • Once in effect, both sides freely choose whether to keep the terms. If the shukenja (or anyone with him) breaks the oath, the creature is freed at once. If the victim tries to break the terms, he is struck with racking pains, losing 1 hit point a round until he gives in or dies.
  • Oaths can be removed by the reverse, unbind, or by atonement.

Material component (oath and unbind): the shukenja's holy symbol.

OA p.63. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

The shukenja projects his spirit into a normal animal (not a monster) with fewer hit dice than he has, forcing it to obey his will. It saves versus spell; if it saves, the spell fails.

  • Possessed, the animal does anything within its ability, whatever the consequences to it.
  • For every point of damage the animal takes, the shukenja takes 1/2 point. If it dies under his control, he must make a system shock roll or die too.
  • Meanwhile his body lies catatonic. If it is disturbed or moved, his spirit is lost until reunited with it, as by a restore spell.

Material components: a bowl of incense and a morsel of food the animal likes.

A more powerful hold person. The wu jen picks the center of the effect, and every creature in the area at that moment saves versus spell; those who fail are transfixed, unable to move, speak, cast spells or act.

  • The wu jen must then state a condition that releases them ("Wait here until I return", "Stay there for all eternity!"). It can be anything, however unlikely; when it is met, they are released automatically.
  • Every six turns they remain transfixed, they get another save versus spell to escape.
  • Creatures entering the area after the casting also save versus spell (at +4) or are transfixed, each time they enter. Creatures removed from the area are freed at once.
  • The spell stays active as long as at least one creature is transfixed.

Material component: a barnacle crushed underfoot when the spell is cast, or a drop of pine resin.

Used only in the face of coming death, it lets the wu jen take one last act of revenge even after being killed. When he is slain, his spirit remains for one round to carry out the last thought fixed in his mind at the moment of death.

  • If a spell is to be used, it must be named clearly. The deed must be something he could have done in one round when he died: not a spell he hadn't memorized or had already cast, or one taking more than a round.
  • If his last thought is unclear, he saves versus death: on a success the player chooses the deed; otherwise the DM decides.
  • The vengeance is aimed at the thing or person that caused his death. His vengeful spirit cares nothing for others' lives and carries out its last deed even if it endangers or harms friends or innocents. If possible it must be carried out; it can't be taken back once announced.
  • The deed is done the next round, and the spirit automatically has initiative over everyone. If the body is there, the spirit reanimates it to do the deed; if not, it appears in ghostly form. The act follows all the normal rules of hitting and saving throws, so it may fail. Success doesn't matter: the spell grants only the chance. Once done, the spirit vanishes and is at rest.

OA p.87. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

A wall of bones erupts from the earth in whatever shape the caster likes within the area. It must stand on solid ground or it collapses into a random pile.

  • It isn't solid but full of small openings and gaps: missiles can be shot through, and those sheltering behind it have 50% cover. Small creatures can wriggle through the openings at 10 feet a round, but the wall is very spiky, and those moving through take 1d8 for every 10 feet.
  • Cast under the feet of creatures, it appears everywhere except where they stand, perhaps trapping them; creatures in the area take 2d8 when it appears.
  • Creatures of strength 18 or more using a blunt weapon can smash it down: every 10 points of damage brings down a 5-foot by 5-foot by 1/2-foot section.
  • It is made of the bones of many kinds of creatures, fused at bizarre angles, and can't be animated by animate dead.

Material component: the branch of a withered peach tree taken from a cemetery.

Element: Fire (OA Table 66).

A blazing curtain of amber flames, doing 2d6 +1 per level of the caster to those within. The side nearest the wu jen gives off no heat; the far side does 1d6 to those within 1" and 1-3 to those within 2". Undead and creatures vulnerable to fire take double damage. The wall can't move. It lasts as long as he concentrates, or rounds equal to his level if he doesn't. It can be a sheet up to 2" square per level, or a ring of 1" + 1/4" per level. Material component: a piece of volcanic glass.

OA p.87. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Grows out of the wu jen's training in meditation and ki: he calms and clears his mind with carefully controlled breathing, releasing the spell's energy. It lets him concentrate on one action whatever else he does; it is one of only two spells (with finding the center) he can cast without breaking concentration on another. He could cast phantasmal force one round and aiming at the target the next without breaking concentration. Once cast, he can move normally, keep his dexterity bonus to armor class, take damage and make saving throws without breaking concentration. His mind stays on the spell he is concentrating on, but he is aware of what happens around him. It lasts two turns or until he stops concentrating on the first spell.

Makes skeletons and zombies from dead bodies, obeying their creator: one skeleton or zombie per level. They last until destroyed or dispelled. Material component: a piece of a burial shroud.

A cone of cold springs from the wu jen's hand, 1/2" long per level. Those in it take 1d4 +1 per level of the wu jen. Material component: a glass cone.

Conjures an elemental of air, water, earth or fire, if a large amount of that element is at hand. It has 16 hit dice and obeys the wu jen while controlled. He must concentrate fully to control it, and even so there is a 5% chance in the second and each following round that control is lost. An uncontrolled elemental attacks the wu jen who summoned it. Control reaches up to 3" per level. Material components by kind: burning incense (air), soft clay (earth), sulfur and phosphorus, lit (fire), water and sand or salt (water). Nature/wood counts as an element but has no elemental creatures.

An amorphous cloud of inky blackness that the caster can shape and move as he likes for the duration, while he concentrates, within range, at 6" a round. It can seep through the smallest cracks and float in the air. No vision passes through it except true sight or similar spells, and it blots out all sound inside, so spellcasters in it can't cast spells that need speech. Wind affects it: for every five miles per hour of wind, the area shrinks by 1 cubic foot and the duration by one round. While concentrating, the wu jen can move no more than 3" a round. Material components: a whisker from an old black cat and a tiny bottle of smoke captured on a moonless night.

Returns an extra-planar creature to its own plane. Its name and type must be known, and the spell must also overcome its magic resistance. The creature saves, with the difference in levels between caster and creature as a bonus or penalty; if it fails (a willing creature needs no save), it is sent home.

The reverse, beckon, calls a creature from another plane to the caster, but doesn't make it friendly. Neither works on natives of the Prime Material Plane, or those with some of their ancestry from it. Material component: for dismissal, something hateful and distasteful to the creature; for beckon, something pleasing and desirable to it.

The wu jen breathes a cone of magic flame: everyone in it takes 1d6 per level unless they save versus breath weapon (for half). Burnable things (other than the clothing and gear of creatures in the cone) catch fire automatically, which may cause more damage to those in the area; the DM rules on these. Material component: a piece of red-hot charcoal held in the caster's teeth, which doesn't harm him.

Gives wood the strength of the finest steel. Only its hardness changes; color, texture and weight are unaffected. Cast on normal living plants, it has a 50% chance of working; if it does, it doesn't interfere with normal growth, but every part of the plant (leaves, flowers and fruit included) has the hardness of steel. A plant-like monster saves versus spell; if it fails, it becomes rigid and paralyzed, its armor class becomes 0, and a to-hit roll is always needed to strike it, since the hardness runs through its whole body. Material component: a pinch of metal filings mixed with willow sap.

Like the 4th level minor creation, but it can create mineral things as well as vegetable ones. Vegetable objects last twice as long.

system.description:

Controls the weight of an item within the size limit, making it too heavy to move or light as a feather; the wu jen can raise it one round and lower it the next, at will. Mass can be raised or lowered by up to 5% per level: at 10th level, by 50%. It doesn't otherwise change the item. Several items in the same 10-foot square can be affected. Missiles can be made up to twice as heavy (doing double normal damage) and still be shot, but their ranges are halved. Heavy things can be carried easily, though bulk may still prevent it: a huge boulder made very light is still hard to carry because of its size. Material components: a hummingbird's feather and a bit of an elephant's toenail.

Element: Earth (OA Table 66).

The skin of a creature touched becomes a gleaming, steel-hard surface: its armor class becomes 2 for the duration, but it grows slow and stiff, moving at half speed and always acting last in combat. Its skin counts as metal for the magnetism spell. Material component: a small piece of rhinoceros hide, swallowed by the caster.

OA p.88. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Element: Earth (OA Table 66).

Opens a passage through wood, plaster or stone walls, 5 feet wide, 8 feet high and 10 feet deep. Material component: a pinch of sesame seeds.

Creates 2d6 +1 per level invisible servants like unseen servant, with all its limits, except that they can also do common labor if carefully directed by the caster: serve at a banquet, help dig earthworks, row a ship, act as porters, or help in a farmer's fields. Material component: a small stick crossbar hung with many lengths of knotted thread.

Creates the illusion of a door or sliding panel that the wu jen seems to step through. In fact he is made invisible for as long as the illusion lasts, and can flee undisturbed. Those opening the "door" see an empty 10-foot by 10-foot room. Only true sight, a gem of seeing or similar means reveals the illusion.

The wu jen sends his spirit out of his body while keeping some semblance of life in it. His spirit separates invisibly and is free to move about; the body doesn't go into a trance but a sort of half-awake state, and he (in spirit form) can have it take simple actions such as walking, talking or eating while he does other things. The body acts as if dazed.

  • In spirit form he can still cast spells, but doing so instantly forces the spirit back to the body. The spirit counts as a spirit for protection from spirits and other spells.
  • Damage to the body or the spirit comes off his hit points. If the body is destroyed, he dies. If it is moved beyond the spell's range, he can't return to it.
  • If the spirit doesn't return before the spell ends, it is trapped outside: the body falls into a catatonic state while the spirit wanders aimlessly, and once the spell has ended he can't cast spells in spirit form. A restore spirit spell returns the spirit to the body.

Material component: a small mandala.

OA p.89. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Element: Earth (OA Table 66).

Forms existing stone into shapes: a stone weapon, a door or trapdoor, a coffer. The carving isn't fine, but rough shapes can be made. Material component: soft clay, worked into the shape wanted.

OA p.89. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

A shimmering pale green blade appears anywhere in range, hovering and dancing in the air and striking by itself while the caster concentrates. It strikes as if wielded by a samurai of the caster's level, for 1d4 damage, and being magical can hit creatures harmed only by magical weapons.

  • Besides the damage, each hit lowers the victim's next saving throw by 1, adding up to -5; beyond that, hits only do damage.
  • It can be moved from creature to creature during the spell, but attacks only one at a time.
  • The penalty stays until the creature must save in a dangerous situation: a companion couldn't cast some harmless spell on him to clear it. Remove curse, limited wish and wish cancel it.

Material components: a miniature sword and a set of loaded dice.

Moves objects by mental concentration: 2" the first round, doubling each round (to a maximum of 1,024" a round). It can move opponents within the weight limit, but those who can move in other ways (such as flying) may escape it if its speed hasn't yet reached 16" a round.

An impenetrable, invisible, immobile barrier where the caster wants it, stopping all blows, attacks and breath weapons in either direction. Only disintegrate, a rod of cancellation or a sphere of annihilation brings it down. Material component: a pinch of diamond powder crushed from stones worth at least 10,000 gp.

Element: Earth (OA Table 66).

A vertical wall of iron, 1/4 inch thick per level and covering 15 square feet per level. Where it can fill a passage tightly, it does; otherwise it may topple, crushing creatures beneath: 50% chance it falls either way, changed by 1% for each 300 lb. over 400, or each point of strength over 30, pushing on it. Material component: an iron bar.

A wall of granite that merges with adjoining rock, 3" thick per level (as printed) and 20 square feet in area per level. It can bridge a chasm, with 50% of its area used for support and buttressing.

Turns water (or any drinkable liquid) into a poison that does 1d4 per level of the caster, half on a successful save versus poison. One swallow is enough. Those smelling the liquid have a 1% chance per level of experience of noticing the poison. Diluted to as little as 50% strength, it does proportionally less damage; diluted further, it only makes drinkers slightly ill. The reverse, poison to water, does the opposite. Material component: the fang of a poisonous snake, dissolved in the liquid to be poisoned or purified.

A sickly pale fire leaps from the caster's fingertips and dances over the wooden target.

  • On a live plant, it works 75% of the time. A plant-like creature saves versus spell to resist. Nonliving wooden things get no save.
  • Once it takes effect, the wood decays at 1 cubic foot per turn; plant-like creatures lose 1 hit die per cubic foot rotted. The rotted wood falls away, crumbling at a touch, until the whole object has rotted. A wooden door can be destroyed in several turns; a large wooden building takes several days.

The reverse, prevent rot, stops the decay caused by wood rot, but doesn't restore wood already decayed. Material component: a live termite (dead, for the reverse).

Reads the aura of an area: the basic alignment and magical tendencies of most of its inhabitants and things. An aura appears over every dwelling or structure in the area, showing whether most of its occupants, or the main one, are good, evil, lawful, neutral or chaotic; areas with a high concentration of magic are shown too. Standing on a hill above a village, the wu jen sees each house glow with the nature of those inside, telling good people, evildoers and lawful folk apart. Temples and shrines glow with magic, since they are more inclined to it, and haunted and cursed places have a fitting aura. It even appears over dwellings the caster can't see directly: a faint glow above the treetops might show a hut or cave deep in the woods. The reverse, mask, hides the aura of one dwelling from this spell.

Changes the weather in an area, taking effect within 1d4 turns of the casting. Each of the three "aspects" of weather (precipitation, temperature and wind) can be moved one degree; the aspects and degrees are explained in the PHB (p.52). Contrary aspects aren't possible. Material component: a small skyrocket.

Makes living, nonliving and magical matter vanish permanently: one creature, or a nonliving object of up to 1" cubic volume. Material component: a lodestone.

Prepares an item for enchantment and brings that about. The item must be sound and undamaged, of the finest materials, costing at least 100 gp.

  • The wu jen works on it alone for 2 + 1d8 days, eight hours a day, to grow familiar with it. He can cast no other spells in that time, and the item must stay within a foot of him.
  • Then he saves; success means the item is ready to receive magic, which must be cast within 24 hours.
  • Each further spell takes 4 + 4-8 hours per spell level, and each must follow within 24 hours of the last.
  • These magics aren't permanent unless a permanency spell is also cast, though items with charges can never be made permanent.

Material component: varies with the item.

The wu jen has no control over what form this takes; he must abide by the winds of fate. 60% chance the result is good, 40% bad.

  • Good: every die roll for the character improves by 1 (or 10% for percentile rolls) for the duration.
  • Bad: his die rolls aren't affected, but he is gripped by a gambling mania for the duration. He automatically accepts any game of chance or wager offered him that has some element of chance (dares don't count). It doesn't force him to accept suicidal bets (he won't agree to kill himself, or let himself be killed, on a coin toss), but he would accept a bet offering freedom or surrender on a roll of the die. He keeps playing any game until he can't pay, though he tries to borrow from others to stay in.

Material component: a small statuette of the god of luck.

Places a magical command on an intelligent, conscious creature to do (or not do) certain things. Self-destructive orders are always ignored, but all others are followed until done. Ignoring the geas makes the target sicken and die within 1d4 weeks, and straying from it costs strength points. Only a wish or similar magic can lift it. The wu jen has only the casting time to phrase it.

Makes 4 inches of metal, 6 feet of stone or 20 feet of wood transparent to the wu jen's gaze, or creates a one-way window. Either way the viewing area is 3 feet wide by 2 feet high, and as strong as the original material. It doesn't work on lead, gold or platinum. Material component: a small piece of crystal.

Lowers water or other fluid by 5% of its current height per level. Material component: a glass vial of dust. The reverse, raise water, raises water to its highest normal level plus 1/2 foot per level of the caster; its component is a vial of water.

The same as the 3rd level suggestion, except that the same suggestion is planted in the minds of a number of creatures. Used on a single creature, its saving throw is at -2.

With a single touch, ferrous metal crumbles into a pile of rust. The wu jen touches the item (rolling to hit if needed), and it falls away in large flakes. Normal metal items get no save; magical metals save versus disintegration (17 for hard metal, 19 for soft metal and jewelry), with a bonus for the strength of their magic. Magic items of iron without a set plus (an iron amulet of ESP, say) get a bonus set by the DM. The reverse, rust to metal, restores a rusted item if at least 90% of the original material is there. Moves dirt, sand and earth (not rock), at one turn of casting for every 4"-square area. Major digging and moving needs an earth elemental's help. Material components: a ball of soil wrapped in a bundle, and a blade of iron.

Aimed at one or more creatures, all within 20 feet of each other. All are struck by pain and agony that passes in an instant, but leaves their muscles knotted and their strength lowered: dexterity and strength drop to 3 for 2d4 rounds, giving -3 to hit, -1 damage, -3 on reaction and attacking adjustment, and +4 to defensive adjustment (worse armor class). Then they return to normal. Strength or prestidigitation ends it, giving the vitality needed to restore normal strength and dexterity. Material components: a leech, and a stone scraped against a slate.

Creates a spectral force that needs no concentration to keep it up.

OA p.91. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Sets up a spectral force that works on command or when set conditions are met, lasting at least one round per level of the caster.

All creatures in the direction the wu jen faces are made to move away at 3" a round. Material component: a pair of statuettes of ebony and ivory.

Like the 3rd level shukenja spell of the same name.

A powerful spell against a creature of the lower planes whose name is known. The material component is a vellum sheet with the incantation and the creature's name written in ink of demon ichor and powdered rubies (1,000 gp for the vellum and 5,000 for the rubies for each document, as printed in gold pieces). Only one such document can exist for a creature at a time, and a wu jen can own only one at a time.

  • If the creature is present, it is rooted to the spot unless it makes its magic resistance roll (if any). If it makes the roll, the reading is so uncomfortable that it flees to its home plane unless held there by magic.
  • In the second round the pain grows, and the creature loses 1 hit point per hit die.
  • In the third round it loses 50% of its remaining hit points and is banished to its home plane for years equal to the caster's level.
  • Most lower-plane creatures hate to be subjected to it, so there is a 25% cumulative chance each round that it gives in to other demands to stop the spell being finished.
  • Either way, the being is the wu jen's sworn foe ever after.

Element: Earth (OA Table 66).

Turns stone to flesh, restoring to life creatures that once lived if they make a system shock roll. Nine cubic feet per level of "unliving" stone can be changed. The reverse turns flesh to stone if the target fails a saving throw. Material components: a pinch of earth and a drop of blood (a pinch of lime and a drop of water for the reverse).

A jet-black sword with a palpable aura of evil appears anywhere in range, aimed at one creature and able to attack only that creature. The wu jen must concentrate on it; it strikes as if he held it himself (non-proficiency penalties don't apply).

  • On a hit it temporarily drains 1-3 levels or hit dice, with the matching hit points, fighting ability, spell levels and level powers. The sword itself does no physical damage.
  • A victim drained below 0 level dies, and in 1-3 days his spirit returns as a kuei (see the OA Lite Monsters).
  • Lost levels return 1-3 turns after the sword vanishes, if the character hasn't died. Lost spells aren't regained, having been wiped from his mind; they must be memorized again.

Material component: a katana or long sword worth at least 100 gp, shattered against a stone.

Like the 5th level shukenja spell true seeing, but it doesn't reveal alignment.

Changes the look of the surrounding area so that the illusion seems real; touch doesn't dispel it. Only true sight, true seeing or similar magic pierces it.

Makes a seaworthy ship from a single sheet of paper; the wu jen needs the origami proficiency. While casting, he folds the sheet into a small junk, then speaks the last words and blows on the paper boat, and in one round it grows into a full-sized sailing ship. It can carry the wu jen and four passengers for every four levels: a 16th level caster could make a small junk for up to 17 man-sized people, a 24th level caster a medium junk for 25. For cargo, one horse counts as four humans, each carrying normal clothing and gear. It needs no crew, moving magically under its own power at 15". At the end of the spell it shrinks back to its original size.

Element: Earth (OA Table 66).

Like warp wood: natural stone buckles and bends as if it were plastic. Walls buckle, stone doors burst their fittings, pillars bend and statues twist. The DM decides the exact effect from the kind of structure and the amount of stone. Material component: a piece of clay twisted in the caster's hands.

The wu jen creates one or more duplicates of himself, with his normal ability scores and personality, carrying his normal equipment but none of his magic items or spell abilities. Their hit points are a quarter of his. They obey him and cooperate with each other, essentially sharing one mind, and can do anything he normally can except cast spells. They take damage like normal characters, but vanish instantly if slain, and each time one dies he takes 10 points of damage. At the end of the spell, all duplicates vanish without harming him. They can't be told from the caster, even by true sight. Material component: a few hairs from his head or beard.

Identical to the 5th level shukenja spell of the same name.

The wu jen becomes two-dimensional, with height and width but no depth. Turned sideways he is invisible, and in this state only true sight or the like can detect him. He can cast spells and move normally, and can't be harmed while invisible, but takes triple damage from attacks while visible in this form. Since he has pushed his depth into the Astral Plane, astral creatures may attack him, with a 25% chance that such an attack draws him fully into the Astral Plane. Material components: a flat likeness of the wu jen carved in ivory, worth 5,000-10,000 gp, and a strip of leather, both used up in the casting.

Summons one of the four kinds of elementals (earth, air, fire or water) and compels it to do a service. Halfway through the casting, a 16 hit die elemental of the right kind appears and the caster states the service.

  • The service must be within the elemental's powers, take no more than one day per level of the wu jen, and be done within its own element: water elementals won't do work that takes them onto land, and fire elementals must stay in their fiery realms.
  • If it saves versus spell, it vanishes at once back to its own plane. If it fails, it tries to carry out the mission. The wu jen needn't supervise; they agree to meet at some set place when it is done.
  • Typical services: a fire elemental forging a blade in the heat of a volcano, a water elemental recovering things from the bottom of the ocean, an earth elemental bringing rare ores from deep in the earth, an air elemental carrying the wu jen somewhere.
  • Once the mission is done and the meeting kept, it returns at once to its plane. Elementals resent being summoned and forced to serve, and may try to take revenge later.

Material components: a large quantity of the element, and a written document stating exactly what service is to be done.

OA p.93. Rewritten in plain words from the page images.

Element: Water (OA Table 66).

Summons fearsome freezing winds, ice and snow over the area.

  • Gray clouds gather and rain begins to drizzle; the temperature falls sharply, 40 degrees in a single day. Winds rise, gently at first and slowly gaining strength. Each day the weather worsens: thicker clouds, heavier rain, colder air, fiercer winds. The temperature can drop no lower than -20 degrees.
  • Snow begins after 6 hours in arctic and winter conditions, by the end of the first day in temperate climes, 36 hours after casting in deserts, and by the end of the second day in the tropics. It then falls at 1 inch an hour to a maximum of 48 inches, whipped into huge drifts (5 to 12 feet or more), with extreme wind chill. During the snowfall, visibility is 20" and movement 1/4 normal.
  • Creatures out in it without warm clothing, fire and shelter take 1d8 each turn. Control weather can't cancel it, but can lessen it by raising the temperature, slowing the snow and breaking the clouds.

Drought, the reverse, cancels ice blight, and otherwise heats and dries the land instead of covering it with snow.

  • The sky quickly clears and stays clear for the duration; no rain falls. The temperature climbs 20 degrees a day, to a maximum of 120 by day and a cool 100 at night.
  • Fields grow hard and cracked after four days. Small streams dry up after six days, and all but the deepest wells after 10. Small rivers shrink to a trickle in 14 days and dry up after 20; large rivers drop noticeably in 10 days and are little more than streams after 20. By the 25th day only extremely deep wells still have water.
  • Plants suffer by size and habitat: desert plants barely notice, while tropical jungles wither and die fast. Normal creatures flee, returning only when normal conditions have come back and the land recovered.
  • Creatures in full sun all day take 2d6 a day without shade and water. Characters in bulky and metal armor take 1-3 a turn from the blistering heat and exhaustion. Control weather can lessen it, and ice blight cancels it automatically.
